newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh jurors confront death penalty issue.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh jurors confront death penalty issue.

text.p: Potential jurors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial publicly wrestled with their consciences on Wednesday over the most private of issues -- whether they could sentence a human to die.

Citizens reporting for possible jury duty in the trial of Timothy McVeigh were forced to confront the question of whether they could vote for the death penalty if the Gulf War veteran is convicted of the April 19, 1995, attack on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building. The blast killed 168 people.
Jurors were even asked if they could look McVeigh, 28, in the eye after voting to send him to his death.
Most admitted that it was the first time in their lives that they thought deeply about the death penalty and for many it was a very uncomfortable experience.

"I've been thinking about this probably through the night last night," said one potential juror, an IBM computer expert, when asked by U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch whether she had strong views on the death penalty.

The woman, finishing testimony begun on Tuesday, said her Christian beliefs would prohibit her from giving McVeigh the death penalty if he was convicted. "I don't feel capable of throwing that first stone ... human justice is imperfect, God's justice is perfect," she said.
A woman who worked on a farm had equally strong views in favour of the death penalty, saying she "would be for the death penalty for anybody that kills other people."
Most jurors said they would be prepared to impose a death penalty if McVeigh were convicted and the evidence justified it.
Anyone sitting in a U.S. death penalty case must be prepared to consider voting for the death penalty. People opposed to capital punishment will be disqualified.

Tom Kight, whose 23-year-old stepdaughter died in the bombing, was sympathetic to the jurors' dilemma. "The fact that you as an individual could be put on a team that would decide a man's fate that could be death I think is a very tough decision," he told reporters.

The pace of jury selection seemed slightly swifter than the snail's pace of the first two days, with Matsch nudging lawyers along and censuring them for repetitious questioning. So far 16 potential jurors have been questioned from a jury panel of 352.
McVeigh, wearing a green shirt and khaki pants, appeared to follow the proceedings closely. Occasionally he whispered to his attorneys and passed notes to them.

McVeigh smiled broadly when one potential juror, a 25-year-old landscaper, talked of his interest in martial arts and looked sombre when another juror, the son of an Air Force general, described his experiences in the Navy which included extensive weapons training and knowledge of nuclear weapons. "I knew every nuke," the juror said.
McVeigh's father, who was in court on the first two days of jury selection to lend moral support to his son, refused to say in interviews whether he believed him to be guilty or innocent.
But he told the Rocky Mountain News on Wednesday that his son's story, as he knows it, has not been told.

In an interview with CBS affliliate KVTV, the elder McVeigh said his son changed after army service and developed a hatred for President Bill Clinton and Attorney General Janet Reno after the government siege of the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, ended in at least 80 deaths.

"If (Tim) is a monster, it is something that happened in the last few years," he told KVTV. In his Rocky Mountain News interview, the elder McVeigh said that when the FBI showed him a sketch and asked if it could be his son, "I told them with his views on the government, it wouldn't surprise me a bit."

McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately later, pleaded not guilty to the attack, which prosecutors said was in revenge for the federal raid on the Branch Davidian sect.
